content: Actinic prurigo, also referred to as Familial polymorphous light eruption of American Indians, Hereditary polymorphous light eruption of American Indians, Hutchinson's summer prurigo, or Hydroa aestivale, is a condition characterized by an itchy, sunlight-induced eruption of papules or nodules on the skin. The condition was first described in 1954 by Escalona in Mexico. The exact cause of actinic prurigo remains unknown. However, researchers suspect that certain proteins in the body may play a role in its development. Ultraviolet (UV) light, specifically UV-A and UV-B, is believed to be the primary trigger for the condition. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that most patients with actinic prurigo live at high altitudes (greater than 1000 meters above sea level), where UV exposure is more intense. Additionally, many patients experience improvement in their symptoms when they relocate to lower altitudes. Actinic prurigo is characterized by intensely itchy, inflamed papules, nodules, and plaques on the skin. These lesions typically appear hours or days after UV light exposure and are most commonly found on sun-exposed areas such as the face, neck, arms, hands, and legs. However, lesions can also develop on areas of the skin that are covered by clothing and not directly exposed to UV light, which can complicate the diagnosis. Actinic prurigo is a chronic condition, and its symptoms often worsen during the spring and summer months when daylight hours increase and UV exposure becomes more frequent. Currently, there is no cure for actinic prurigo. Treatment focuses on managing the dermatologic symptoms through the use of topical steroid creams or systemic immunosuppressants. Commonly prescribed treatments include topical creams such as tacrolimus and betamethasone, as well as systemic medications like prednisone. In some cases, thalidomide has been shown to effectively control the symptoms of actinic prurigo. Patients with actinic prurigo are strongly advised to minimize sun exposure and to use high-SPF sunscreen consistently throughout the year, even on cloudy or overcast days. This is because UV-A light, unlike UV-B light, can penetrate cloud cover and remains constant throughout the day. Alternative treatment approaches may include UV hardening therapy, meditation, and cognitive behavioral therapy. UV-A desensitization phototherapy has also demonstrated effectiveness in some cases. However, it is important to note that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not yet approved these alternative treatments, and further research is needed to better understand this condition and its management in the United States.
